question: What is the meaning of industrial symbiosis markets in relation to interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)?
data_group: interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)
description: Industrial symbiosis markets in relation to interactive decision support tools refer to the interconnected relationships between different industries where waste from one process becomes a resource for another, promoting sustainability and resource efficiency. Interactive decision support tools in this context are tools that aid in exploring and making decisions related to Circular Economy (CE) object governance, facilitating informed choices and strategies for managing resources effectively within industrial symbiosis markets.

2.1. Industry 4.0 as enabler of CE in the manufacturing sector and its relation to MPs
The integration of Industry 4.0 (I4.0 ) technologies and supply chain innovations is crucial for advancing the transition to a Circular 
Economy (CE) within the manufacturing sector. Technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain, artificial intelligence 
(AI), and big data analytics offer practical solutions to optimize supply chain processes and foster more sustainable manufacturing 
practices. In doing so, they enable the principles of CE by promoting resource efficiency, extending product lifecycles, and reducing 
waste [43].
Among these technologies, IoT stands out as a key driver for implementing CE in manufacturing. IoT devices provide real-time data 
on the condition of equipment and products throughout their lifecycle. This capability allows manufacturers to ensure that resources 
are used efficiently and to implement predictive maintenance strategies, thereby reducing downtime and prolonging the lifespan of 
machinery [51]. By collecting and analysing data from IoT-enabled devices, manufacturers gain valuable insights into product per­
formance and wear patterns, which can inform the design of more durable and repairable products. Additionally, IoT enhances the 
traceability of products across the supply chain, a crucial element for identifying items that can be refurbished, remanufactured, or 
recycled, thereby preventing valuable materials from becoming waste [24]. Blockchain technology is another transformative tool that 
supports CE by improving transparency and traceability within supply chains. Blockchain creates immutable records of key infor­
mation about a product’s origin, composition, and lifecycle status, making it easier to verify compliance with sustainability standards 
[33]. This transparency fosters greater accountability across supply chain stakeholders and enhances consumer trust in sustainable 
products. Furthermore, blockchain enables the use of smart contracts, which can automatically trigger actions such as recycling or 
refurbishment when predefined conditions are met, simplifying the execution of CE processes [61].
AI and big data analytics also play essential roles in advancing CE within manufacturing. These technologies enable the processing 
of large volumes of data to identify inefficiencies and opportunities for resource optimization [4]. For instance, AI algorithms can 
predict future demand patterns, helping manufacturers adjust production levels to avoid overproduction and reduce waste. Similarly, 
big data analytics provides insights into material flows within and between industries, facilitating opportunities for industrial sym­
biosis, a key concept of CE where waste from one process becomes an input for another [76]. Additionally, digital twins, a core 
I4.0 technology, offer additional opportunities for promoting CE in manufacturing. A digital twin is a virtual representation of a 
physical asset, providing real-time data on its condition and performance. By using digital twins, manufacturers can simulate changes 
in processes before implementing them in the physical world, reducing the risk of errors and waste. In the context of CE, digital twins 
can model the lifecycle of products to identify ways to extend their lifespan through repair, refurbishment, or remanufacturing [58]. 
This predictive capability ensures that resources are used more efficiently and that products remain in circulation for longer periods, 
aligning with CE principles.
Incorporating I4.0 technologies into supply chain management also facilitates more effective reverse logistics processes, where 
products and materials are returned to manufacturers for reuse or recycling. Effective reverse logistics requires detailed knowledge of a 
product’s composition and lifecycle status, information that I4.0 technologies can provide through real-time data tracking and 
analysis. Additionally, digital supply chains improve collaboration between stakeholders, enabling the development of circular 
business models such as product-as-a-service. In this model, manufacturers retain ownership of their products and take responsibility 
for managing them at the end of their lifecycle, ensuring that valuable materials are recovered and reintegrated into the supply chain 
[66].
In the BE, MPs further illustrate how I4.0 technologies can promote CE. MPs are digital documents that contain detailed infor­
mation about building materials, including their origin, properties, and potential for reuse. Blockchain technology ensures that the 
information contained in MPs is secure and tamper-proof, enhancing trust in sustainable building practices. Meanwhile, IoT devices 
embedded in building materials can update MPs with real-time data on the condition of materials, enabling proactive maintenance and 
extending their lifespan. Digital twins further support MPs by allowing construction professionals to simulate how materials can be 
reused in future projects, minimizing waste and promoting resource efficiency.

2.2. Data management and Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) in Building Information Modelling (BIM). How are they related to MPs?
BIM models encompass more than just visual representations; they contain critical information that aids stakeholders in accessing, 
evaluating, and utilizing data effectively with proper management [34]. However, due to the fact that there are many software tools 
could lead to significant compatibility challenges. Efficient collaboration and data interchange between the various stakeholders is 
made possible by open standards like Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) and effective data management procedures [1]. BIM models 
constantly change as a result of contributions from the different stakeholders during the course of the project. Version control is 
ensured by effective data management, allowing teams to monitor changes and operate with the most recent data, improving 
transparency and eliminating mistakes [34]. With this variety of contributors to BIM models, data integrity is essential. In order to 
promote the stakeholders’ confidence in decision-making, rigorous data management protocols are required to provide consistent 
information. This is achieved through the building’s lifespan, as efficiency and sustainability are improved, supported by useful in­
sights through the data-rich environment of BIM [1,34].
For the reasons mentioned above, BuildingSMART created the open IFC standard, which allows easier exchange of building data 
models between the different BIM software platforms and promotes easier cooperation and communication with the various stake­
holders. In contrast to vendor-specific proprietary formats, IFC fosters vendor-neutrality and interoperability, enabling project teams 
to use their favourite tools without sacrificing data integrity [34]. Comprehensive information about 3D geometry, attributes,
